title: Capstone: An Argument from the Texts
bigQuestion: How do you build a fair, well-sourced argument about a hard passage for readers who may believe differently?

story.title: Three Texts on a Table
story.kicker: A senior lays out Genesis 6, 1 Enoch 6 and Jude 14 and begins to write.
paragraphs: It was the first week of spring break, and Darius had the dining table to himself. He laid out three printed pages side by side. On the left was Genesis 6:1–4 in the King James Version. In the middle was chapter 6 of 1 Enoch in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation. On the right was the short letter of Jude, with verses 14 and 15 marked in pencil.

His capstone question was written on a card above them: Who are the sons of God in Genesis 6? He had read two researchers. Michael Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), read them as heavenly beings. George Nickelsburg's commentary on 1 Enoch (2001) treated 1 Enoch 6–11 as an early Jewish expansion of the same verses. He had also read that Augustine, centuries earlier, answered differently. His teacher had asked for one clear thesis, the texts behind it, at least two researchers' readings stated fairly, and a calm presentation.

Darius began by drawing lines between the pages. Genesis spoke of sons of God and the Nephilim. 1 Enoch told a longer story of two hundred Watchers who came down on Mount Hermon. Jude quoted a prophecy of Enoch, in words very close to 1 Enoch 1:9. He wrote a note: Jude knew this book. Then a second note: knowing a book is not the same as treating it as Scripture. Readers disagree about that.

He opened a blank document and typed a first sentence, then deleted it. It sounded too sure. He tried again: The oldest surviving readers of Genesis 6, such as 1 Enoch and Jubilees, read the sons of God as heavenly beings, while Augustine and Genesis Rabbah read them as men. That sentence named the documents and said who read them which way. He left it and kept writing.
story.think: Why did Darius delete his first sentence? What makes the second version stronger for readers who may not share any one researcher's view?

lessons.title: A Question the Texts Can Answer
lessons.mainIdea: A strong capstone question is narrow, open to more than one reading, and answerable from texts you can cite.
reading: Every capstone starts with a *research question*: the single question your paper sets out to answer. Some questions are too big, such as What is the unseen realm? Others cannot be answered from texts at all, such as Are angels real? A strong question points to specific passages, has more than one serious answer, and can be argued from evidence a reader can check.

Compare two versions. Weak: What did ancient people think about giants? Strong: Who are the sons of God in Genesis 6:1–4? The second names a passage, has at least three well-known readings, and lets you gather evidence from Genesis, 1 Enoch, the New Testament and later interpreters. The limits of a question are called its *scope*. A narrow scope lets you go deep.

Your answer to the question is your *thesis*: one sentence you will defend. In this course a thesis is about what a text says or how a reader interprets it, not about what anyone should believe. The Dead Sea Scroll reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 is older than the Masoretic reading is a thesis you can test. The Bible is true or false is not, and it is not the work of this paper.

words.d: the single question a paper or project sets out to answer
the limits of a question: which texts, readers and period it covers
a one-sentence answer to the research question, which the paper defends with evidence

look.title: Sort the Questions
look.text: 1. What does the Book of the Watchers add to Genesis 6? 2. Is the supernatural real? 3. What does Deuteronomy 32:8 say in the oldest copies? 4. What do all religions teach about spirits? 5. Is 1 Peter 3:19 about the Watchers?
look.prompt: Which of these questions can be argued from texts you can cite in one paper? For each question you reject, say why: too big, or not answerable from texts.

check.q: Which is the strongest capstone research question?
choices: What did everyone in history think about giants?
Who are the sons of God in Genesis 6:1–4?
check.why: It names a passage, has several serious readings, and can be argued from citable texts.

check.q: What is a thesis?
choices: A one-sentence answer the paper defends with evidence
check.why: A thesis answers the research question in one sentence and is supported with evidence.

check.q: Why is The Bible is true not a thesis for this paper?
choices: It is about belief, not about what a text says or how a reader interprets it
check.why: The capstone studies texts and readings. It does not argue for or against any faith claim.

lessons.title: Five Model Questions
lessons.mainIdea: Five questions from this course make strong capstones, because each rests on specific texts with more than one reading.
reading: Question one: Who are the sons of God in Genesis 6? 1 Enoch, Jubilees and Josephus read them as heavenly beings. Julius Africanus and Augustine read them as Seth's line, and Genesis Rabbah as judges or nobles. Question two: What does Deuteronomy 32:8 say in the oldest copies? The Masoretic Text reads sons of Israel, while a Dead Sea Scroll reads sons of God.

Question three: Is 1 Peter 3:19 about the Watchers? The verse says Christ preached to the spirits in prison, who disobeyed in the days of Noah. Many modern commentators read these as the imprisoned angels of Genesis 6, as 1 Enoch describes them. Others read the verse as Christ speaking through Noah to the people of his day, or as a message to the dead.

Question four: What did Jesus do at Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon? Heiser, in Reversing Hermon (2017), traced a *motif*, a repeated image or theme, from 1 Enoch's Hermon to Matthew 16. Other readers see the setting as simply where the scene took place. Question five: Where do demons come from in 1 Enoch and in the Gospels? 1 Enoch 15 answers; the Gospels do not say. Whichever you pick, write down the *key passages* before you read any commentary.

words.d: a repeated image or theme that links several texts, such as a sacred mountain
the few texts, cited by book, chapter and verse, on which a question mainly depends
the phrase in 1 Peter 3:19 for those to whom Christ preached, read in several different ways

look.title: Match the Question to Its Texts
look.text: Texts: Genesis 6:1–4. Deuteronomy 32:8–9. 1 Peter 3:18–22. 2 Peter 2:4. Jude 6 and 14–15. 1 Enoch 6 and 15. Matthew 16:13–18. Justin, Second Apology 5. Questions: sons of God; Deuteronomy 32:8; 1 Peter 3:19; Caesarea Philippi; where demons come from.
look.prompt: Assign each text to the question or questions it helps answer. Which text is useful for more than one question, and why?

check.q: According to 1 Peter 3:19–20, when were the spirits in prison disobedient?
check.why: 1 Peter 3:20 links the spirits to disobedience in the days of Noah.

check.q: What is a motif?
choices: A repeated image or theme that links several texts
check.why: A motif, such as the sacred mountain Hermon, recurs across texts.

check.q: Which early readers took the sons of God in Genesis 6 as heavenly beings?
check.why: 1 Enoch, Jubilees and Josephus read them as angels; the others read them as men.

lessons.title: Genesis 6 Beside 1 Enoch 6
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch 6 retells Genesis 6 at length, and it is one of the earliest witnesses to how Jewish readers understood the sons of God.
reading: Genesis 6:1–4 is only four verses long. It says the sons of God saw that human daughters were beautiful and took wives, and it mentions the Nephilim and the mighty men of old. It does not name the sons of God, explain where they came from or tell what happened next. Every reader has to fill in something.

*1 Enoch* fills in a great deal. It is a collection of Jewish writings, with its oldest parts dating to the 200s BCE or earlier. Aramaic fragments of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Its first part, the Book of the Watchers (chapters 1–36), tells that two hundred *Watchers*, angels of heaven, came down on the summit of Mount Hermon, led by Semjaza, and bound themselves by an oath.

For a capstone, 1 Enoch is evidence of interpretation. It shows how some Jewish writers read Genesis 6 in the centuries before Jesus. Nickelsburg's commentary, 1 Enoch 1 (2001), studies chapters 6–11 as one of the earliest expansions of Genesis 6, and many researchers agree it is a key early witness. 1 Enoch is part of the Bible only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches. Other traditions read it as an ancient book outside Scripture.

words.d: a collection of ancient Jewish writings, parts of it from the 200s BCE or earlier, canonical in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings who came down to earth against God's order
the beings named in Genesis 6:2 and 6:4, read as heavenly beings, Sethites or kings by different readers
the first part of 1 Enoch, chapters 1–36, which retells Genesis 6

look.title: The Watchers on Hermon
look.text: The angels, the children of heaven, saw the daughters of men and chose to take wives from among them. Their leader Semjaza feared he alone would pay for the deed, so all of them swore an oath together. They were two hundred in all, and they came down in the days of Jared on the summit of Mount Hermon.
look.cite: 1 Enoch 6:1–6, after R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917), paraphrased
look.prompt: Which details here are not in Genesis 6:1–4? List three, and say why a careful paper labels them as 1 Enoch's retelling.

check.q: How many Watchers does 1 Enoch 6 say came down?
check.why: 1 Enoch 6 counts two hundred Watchers, who came down on Mount Hermon.

check.q: Where does 1 Enoch place the Watchers' descent?
check.why: 1 Enoch 6:6 places the descent on the summit of Mount Hermon.

check.q: Which churches include 1 Enoch in their Bible?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
check.why: 1 Enoch is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

lessons.title: Deuteronomy 32:8 in Three Witnesses
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 32:8 reads sons of Israel in the Masoretic Text but sons of God in a Dead Sea Scroll, and researchers build different pictures on it.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:8 describes God dividing the nations and setting their borders. The *Masoretic Text* says he set them according to the number of the sons of Israel. The King James Version follows it. But a Dead Sea Scroll copy of Deuteronomy, known as 4QDeut-j, reads sons of God. Many Septuagint manuscripts read angels of God, and some read sons of God.

Comparing such witnesses to find the most likely original wording is called *textual criticism*. Many textual critics judge sons of God to be the older reading. They think later scribes likely changed it to avoid any hint of other heavenly beings sharing in God's rule. Several modern translations now print sons of God in this verse, with a note.

Researchers who accept that reading still build different pictures on it. Mark S. Smith, in The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (2001), reads verses 8–9 as a trace of an older view in which the Most High and the LORD were once distinct. Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), reads them as one God who placed the nations under lesser heavenly beings and kept Israel for himself. Readers who prefer the Masoretic reading link the verse instead to the seventy nations of Genesis 10.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Hebrew Bible, copied with great care by Jewish scribes in the Middle Ages
comparing manuscripts and translations to find the most likely original wording of a text
ancient Jewish manuscripts, many from the last centuries BCE, found near the Dead Sea from 1947 on

look.title: Deuteronomy 32:8 in the KJV
look.text: When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 32:8, King James Version (1611), following the Masoretic Text
look.prompt: Which phrase would change if the translators had followed the Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-j? How would that one change matter for Smith's and Heiser's readings?

check.q: What does the Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-j read in Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: 4QDeut-j reads sons of God, where the Masoretic Text reads sons of Israel.

check.q: What is textual criticism?
choices: Writing a review of a book
Comparing manuscripts to find the most likely original wording
check.why: Textual criticism weighs manuscripts and translations to recover the likely original wording.

check.q: How do Smith and Heiser differ on Deuteronomy 32:8–9?
choices: Smith rejects the Qumran reading; Heiser accepts it
Smith sees a trace of the Most High and the LORD as once distinct; Heiser reads them as one God
Both read the verse as about Seth
Heiser reads sons of Israel; Smith reads angels
check.why: Both accept sons of God, but Smith (2001) and Heiser (2015) read verses 8–9 differently.

lessons.title: Peter, Jude and Tartarus
lessons.mainIdea: 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6 and Jude 14–15 show New Testament writers using themes found in 1 Enoch, and many readers use them to read 1 Peter 3:19.
reading: Three short New Testament passages matter for the Watchers question. 2 Peter 2:4 says God did not spare the angels who sinned but held them in chains of darkness for judgment. The Greek verb there is built on *Tartarus*, the name Greek writers gave to the deepest prison of the underworld. Jude 6 says angels who left their proper dwelling are kept in chains under darkness.

Jude 14–15 goes further. It says that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied that the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones to judge. These words closely match 1 Enoch 1:9, and researchers broadly agree on the link. Richard Bauckham's commentary, Jude, 2 Peter (1983), studies how Jude draws on 1 Enoch. Readers differ over what the quotation means: some say Jude treated the book as authoritative, others that he quoted a text his readers valued, as Paul once quoted Greek poets.

These passages matter for 1 Peter 3:19. If 2 Peter and Jude speak of sinning angels held in chains, then the spirits in prison of 1 Peter could be the same beings. Many modern commentators read it that way, and some read Christ's preaching as a proclamation of victory over them. Other readers hold that 1 Peter speaks of Christ speaking through Noah, and the link to Jude is a separate question.

words.d: in Greek thought the deepest prison of the underworld; 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb built on this word
a short New Testament letter that, in verses 14–15, quotes words closely matching 1 Enoch 1:9
a public announcement; some readers take 1 Peter 3:19 as Christ announcing victory, not offering a second chance

look.title: 2 Peter 2:4
look.text: For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment;
look.cite: 2 Peter 2:4, King James Version (1611); the Greek verb for cast down to hell is built on Tartarus
look.prompt: The KJV writes hell here. Why might a capstone paper note the Greek word Tartarus instead? What link to 1 Enoch does that word help a reader see?

check.q: Which 1 Enoch verse does Jude 14–15 closely match?
check.why: Jude 14–15 closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9, the prophecy of the Lord coming with his holy ones.

check.q: What is Tartarus?
choices: The deepest prison of the underworld in Greek thought
check.why: 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb built on Tartarus, the Greek name for the deepest prison of the underworld.

check.q: Which commentary studies how Jude draws on 1 Enoch?
choices: Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (2001)
check.why: Richard Bauckham's Jude, 2 Peter (1983) examines Jude's use of 1 Enoch.

lessons.title: Hermon and Caesarea Philippi
lessons.mainIdea: Matthew sets Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon, and readers differ over whether the setting carries meaning.
reading: *Mount Hermon* is the tallest mountain in the region, on the northern edge of ancient Israel. 1 Enoch 6 places the Watchers' descent on its summit. At its foot lay the town of *Caesarea Philippi*, known for a cave shrine to the Greek god Pan. Matthew 16:13–18 sets a famous scene there. Jesus asks his disciples who he is, and Peter answers that he is the Christ.

Jesus then speaks of building his church, and says the gates of hell, in Greek the gates of Hades, will not prevail against it. In Reversing Hermon (2017), Heiser argued that the setting was chosen on purpose. Near a mountain linked with rebellion in 1 Enoch and a shrine to another god, Jesus announces a new community that the powers of death cannot hold back. He also thought the high mountain of the Transfiguration, in the next chapter, was Hermon.

Other readers weigh this differently. An old Christian tradition places the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor, in Galilee. Many scholars read the gates of Hades as the power of death in general, without a link to the Watchers. A capstone on this question should state each reading in full, then show where Matthew's text supports it and where it is silent.

words.d: the tallest mountain on the northern edge of ancient Israel, where 1 Enoch places the Watchers' descent
a town at the foot of Mount Hermon, known for a shrine to Pan, where Matthew 16 sets Peter's confession
the phrase in Matthew 16:18 for the power of death or the underworld; the KJV renders it gates of hell

look.title: Matthew 16:18
look.text: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
look.prompt: Some readers link this verse to its setting near Hermon. What would you need to show from Matthew 16:13 and from 1 Enoch 6 to support that reading?

check.q: Where does Matthew 16 set Peter's confession?
check.why: Matthew 16:13 places the scene in the region of Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon.

check.q: Where does an old Christian tradition place the Transfiguration?
check.why: Tradition names Mount Tabor in Galilee; Heiser and some others argued for Hermon.

check.q: What is the Greek phrase behind the KJV's gates of hell in Matthew 16:18?
check.why: The Greek reads gates of Hades, often read as the power of death.

lessons.title: Stating a Reading Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: Present each researcher's reading in its strongest form, in your own words, with the book and year.
reading: A fair paper states an argument so well that the person who made it would agree with the summary. Some call this the *charitable reading*: presenting a view at its strongest before you weigh it. That means giving a researcher's main texts, reasons and conclusion, not a weaker version that is easy to knock down. The capstone asks you to do this for at least two researchers.

Here is an example for Genesis 6. Nickelsburg, in his 1 Enoch commentary (2001), reads 1 Enoch 6–11 as an early expansion of Genesis 6:1–4 that uses the story to speak about violence and evil in its own day. Heiser, in The Unseen Realm (2015), argues that sons of God names heavenly beings, as in Job 1:6 and 38:7. He places the passage in a wider biblical theme of heavenly rebellion.

Notice what the example does. It names each source and year. It uses verbs like reads and argues, which keep each idea attached to its author. It gives the evidence, so readers can check it. It does not quote either book, because modern books are under *copyright*; it puts their ideas in your own words, and that is the right way to handle them.

words.d: presenting someone's view at its strongest before weighing it
the legal right of an author or publisher to control copying of a work for a period of time
a restatement of an idea in your own words, with the source named

look.title: Strong or Weak?
look.text: Version 1: Scholars who read Genesis 6 as angels just believed an old book. Version 2: Early readers such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees and Josephus took sons of God as heavenly beings. Some modern researchers add that the same phrase names heavenly beings in Job 1:6 and 38:7.
look.prompt: Which version would a researcher who holds the angel reading recognize as their own argument? Name two things the weaker version leaves out.

check.q: What is a charitable reading?
choices: Presenting a view at its strongest before weighing it
check.why: A charitable reading states an argument so its author would recognize it.

check.q: Where else does sons of God name heavenly beings, according to the angel reading?
check.why: Job 1:6 and 38:7 use the phrase for heavenly beings, which angel-reading scholars cite for Genesis 6.

check.q: Why should a paper paraphrase modern scholars rather than quote them?
choices: Their books are under copyright, so you put their ideas in your own words and cite them
Quoting is never allowed in any paper
check.why: Modern books are under copyright. A paraphrase with the book and year is the right way to use them.

lessons.title: Stating Other Readings Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: Name the other main readings, with their ancient sources, and present each with the same care.
reading: A capstone must also present the main readings you do not hold. For Genesis 6, the *Sethite view* is the best known in Christian history. Julius Africanus offered it in the early 200s, and Augustine, in The City of God 15.23 around 420 CE, made it the leading reading. The sons of God are the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men the line of Cain. The sin was a mixing of faithful and unfaithful families.

Jewish tradition offers another reading. Genesis Rabbah 26, a rabbinic commentary compiled around the 400s CE, records the view that the sons of God were sons of judges. Targum Onqelos, an Aramaic translation, reads sons of the great ones. This is often called the *royal view*: the sin was powerful men taking whomever they wished.

Each reading has reasons. The Sethite view fits Genesis 4–5, where Cain's and Seth's lines are listed. The royal view fits the ancient practice of calling rulers sons of a god. The angel reading fits Job and 1 Enoch. A fair paper states each reading's best evidence, then weighs them, using the same *criteria* for all.

words.d: the reading, taught by Augustine and others, that the sons of God were the godly line of Seth
the reading, found in rabbinic sources, that the sons of God were judges, nobles or kings
a rabbinic commentary on Genesis, compiled around the 400s CE
the standards used to judge between readings, applied equally to each

look.title: Books in Different Bibles
look.cite: Standard canon lists; the Ethiopian Orthodox count varies by how books are grouped
look.prompt: Only one of these canons includes 1 Enoch. How might that affect how much weight different readers give 1 Enoch in reading Genesis 6?

check.q: Who made the Sethite view the leading reading in The City of God?
check.why: Augustine, in The City of God (early 400s CE), read the sons of God as the line of Seth.

check.q: What does the royal view say about the sons of God?
choices: They were the line of Seth
They were judges, nobles or kings
check.why: The royal view, found in Genesis Rabbah and some Aramaic translations, reads them as powerful men.

check.q: What should a fair paper do with criteria?
choices: Apply the same criteria to every reading
Skip criteria for the reading you prefer
Use them only in the conclusion
Use stricter ones for views it dislikes
check.why: Fair weighing uses the same standards for every reading.

lessons.title: Weighing the Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Weigh readings by the age of the witnesses, the fit with context, and how much of the evidence each reading explains.
reading: Once the readings are stated, weigh them. Four questions help. How old are the witnesses for each reading? How well does each reading fit the passage's own *context*? How early do other readers support it? And how much of the evidence does it explain without strain? A reading that explains more evidence, more simply, has a stronger case.

Apply these to Genesis 6. The heavenly-beings reading has early witnesses: 1 Enoch, parts of which date to the 200s BCE or earlier, and the Septuagint tradition that renders Nephilim as giants. The Sethite view appears later, in Christian writers such as Julius Africanus and Augustine. Supporters of the Sethite view answer that it fits the family lists in Genesis 4–5 and avoids reading angels as able to marry.

Weighing is not the same as deciding what is true about God or the unseen world. It is a judgment about which reading best explains a text. Your conclusion can be firm, measured or open: the evidence favors, the evidence is divided, or more study is needed. Each can be a strong *conclusion* if it follows honestly from what you have shown.

words.d: the surrounding words, history and culture that shape what a passage means
any manuscript, translation or early writer that shows how a text read or was read
the paper's final judgment, stated as firmly as the evidence allows

look.title: The Five Parts of 1 Enoch
look.cite: 1 Enoch, divisions as in R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917)
look.prompt: The part that retells Genesis 6 is the longest. Why does it matter for a Genesis 6 paper to cite the Book of the Watchers, not just 1 Enoch as a whole?

check.q: Which is one of the four weighing questions in the lesson?
choices: Which reading does my family hold?
How old are the witnesses for each reading?
Which reading is most popular online?
check.why: The age of the witnesses is one of the four questions, with context, early support and explanatory power.

check.q: Which part of 1 Enoch retells Genesis 6?
check.why: The Book of the Watchers, chapters 1–36, retells the story of Genesis 6.

check.q: What does weighing the evidence decide in this capstone?
choices: Which reading best explains the text
Whether the unseen world is real
Whether a scholar was a good person
check.why: Weighing judges which reading best explains a text, not what is true about God or the unseen world.

lessons.title: Building the Argument
lessons.mainIdea: A capstone paper moves from thesis to evidence to counterargument to conclusion, and cites every text by book, chapter, verse and translation.
reading: A clear paper follows a simple order. The introduction states the question and your thesis. The body presents the key passages and what they say. Next come the readings: at least two researchers', such as Reed and Stuckenbruck on the Watchers' later history, each with its evidence. Then the weighing. Last, the conclusion restates the thesis and says how firmly the evidence supports it.

A strong paper includes a *counterargument*: the best case against your thesis, answered fairly. If you argue that 1 Peter 3:19 refers to the Watchers, give the strongest case for the Noah reading, then explain why you still hold your view, or why the question stays open. Readers trust a writer who faces the hard evidence.

Every *citation* names the text and the translation. Write Genesis 6:4, King James Version (1611), or 1 Enoch 6:6, R. H. Charles (1917), or Reed, Fallen Angels and the History of Judaism and Christianity (2005), paraphrased. Quote only public-domain translations exactly, and mark everything else as a paraphrase. Never invent a page number, quotation or statistic.

words.d: the strongest case against your thesis, which your paper states and answers fairly
a note naming exactly where a quotation or idea comes from, with the translation
works no longer under copyright, such as the King James Version (1611), which anyone may quote

look.title: One Paper in Outline
look.text: Question: Is 1 Peter 3:19 about the Watchers? Thesis: The evidence leans toward the Watchers reading. Evidence: 1 Peter 3:18–22; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6; 1 Enoch 10. Reading 1: a proclamation to imprisoned angels. Reading 2: Christ spoke through Noah. Weighing: context of Noah in 3:20; links to 2 Peter and Jude. Conclusion: leans, with reasons.
look.prompt: Where in this outline should the counterargument go? Write the one sentence that would introduce it.

check.q: What is a counterargument in a capstone paper?
choices: A summary of your own thesis
The strongest case against your thesis, stated and answered fairly
check.why: A counterargument presents the best case against your view and answers it.

check.q: Which citation follows this lesson's model?
check.why: It names the book, chapter, verse and translation with its year, and invents no page number.

check.q: In the lesson's order, what comes right after the key passages?
choices: A list of every book on the topic
At least two researchers' readings, each with its evidence
check.why: After presenting the passages, the paper states at least two researchers' readings.

lessons.title: Presenting to Readers Who Differ
lessons.mainIdea: Present calmly and respectfully, attribute every view, and let listeners of every background follow the evidence.
reading: Your audience may include classmates who are Christian, Jewish, of another faith or of none. Some may hold one of the readings you present; some may never have heard of any of them. A good presentation lets all of them follow the evidence. It uses *neutral language*: words that report a view without mocking it or pushing the listener to adopt it.

Attribution does most of the work. Say Nickelsburg reads, Augustine read, Genesis Rabbah records, 1 Enoch tells. Avoid we for any faith, and avoid telling listeners what they should believe. Show the key passages on screen with their translation, so everyone reads the same words. Speak slowly, and keep each slide to one idea.

Questions from the audience are part of the work. If someone disagrees, thank them and ask which text or witness they would weigh differently. That turns a disagreement into a shared look at the evidence. Showing *respectful disagreement* suits this subject: the texts are old, the readings are many, and careful people still reach different conclusions.

words.d: the people who hear or read your work, often from many backgrounds
words that report a view without mocking it or pushing the listener to adopt it
differing with someone while treating them and their view with care and fairness

look.title: A Question From the Floor
look.text: After a presentation on Deuteronomy 32:8, a classmate says: I was taught the Masoretic Text is the most reliable, so sons of Israel must be right. The presenter has thirty seconds to answer.
look.prompt: Write a calm answer that thanks the classmate, names the two readings and their witnesses, and invites them to weigh the evidence together.

check.q: What is neutral language?
choices: Speaking without any opinions at all
Words that report a view without mocking it or pushing the listener to adopt it
check.why: Neutral language reports views fairly, so listeners of every background can follow.

check.q: Which sentence fits a respectful presentation?
choices: Anyone who disagrees has not read the text
We know the Watchers were real
1 Enoch reads the sons of God as heavenly beings, while Augustine read them as Seth's line
check.why: It attributes each view to its reader and ranks neither.

check.q: How should a presenter respond when a listener disagrees?
choices: Thank them and ask which text or witness they would weigh differently
check.why: Asking about the evidence turns a disagreement into a shared look at the texts.

review.q: Which makes a strong capstone research question?
choices: It has one answer everyone accepts
It is about whether a faith is true
It covers every text in the Bible
It names specific passages and has more than one serious reading
review.why: A strong question is narrow, open to more than one reading and answerable from citable texts.

review.q: What reading does 4QDeut-j give in Deuteronomy 32:8?
review.why: The Dead Sea Scroll reads sons of God; the Masoretic Text reads sons of Israel.

review.q: Which New Testament passage closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9?
review.why: Jude 14–15 presents a prophecy of Enoch that closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9.

review.q: Why does Matthew 16 matter to readers who link it with 1 Enoch?
choices: It was where the Septuagint was made
It is set at Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon, where 1 Enoch places the Watchers' descent
It was the site of the tower of Babel
review.why: Caesarea Philippi sits at the foot of Hermon, which 1 Enoch 6 links with the Watchers.

review.q: How do the Sethite and royal views differ?
choices: The royal view reads the line of Seth; the Sethite view reads kings
The Sethite view reads the line of Seth; the royal view reads judges, nobles or kings
review.why: Augustine's Sethite view reads Seth's line; the royal view in Genesis Rabbah reads sons of judges.

review.q: What must the capstone include about researchers?
choices: At least two researchers' readings, each stated fairly with book and year
review.why: The capstone states at least two researchers' readings, paraphrased and cited.

review.q: Which is a well-formed citation for 2 Peter 2:4?
review.why: A citation gives book, chapter, verse and translation with its year.

review.q: Which conclusion follows the chapter's advice on weighing?
choices: The evidence leans toward one reading, for reasons stated
The other reading is obviously silly
review.why: A conclusion judges which reading best explains a text, stated as firmly as the evidence allows.
